title: How Black Boxes Work
summary: Josh and Chuck explain black boxes in aviation: the flight data recorder, cockpit voice recorder, and crash survivable memory unit that together make up the so-called black box. They cover the history (V. A. Hoff-era flight recording, David Warren's cockpit voice recorder after a mysterious crash, Australian mandates), the shift from magnetic tape to solid-state memory, what sensors and microphones feed the recorders, why they sit in the tail, the crash survivability testing (impact, pin drop, static crush, fire, deep-sea and saltwater immersion), underwater locator beacon pings, recovery of Air France Flight 447 data after two years, how investigators reconstruct crashes, and black box-style recorders in cars and trains. The episode opens with a listener request from Cormack and closes with a listener mail item about kosher meat and salt.

segments.title: Opening banter and listener request
segments.summary: Hosts introduce the episode as a request from a young listener, Cormack, and briefly ask a listener to contact them about day planners.

segments.title: What black boxes are and history of flight recording
segments.summary: Hosts clarify that black boxes are orange, not black, and that the term covers the flight data recorder, cockpit voice recorder, and crash survivable memory unit. They trace early flight recording, including a 1940s Finnish engineer and a possible Wright Brothers propeller recorder, and Australian David Warren, who added cockpit audio after a mysterious crash.

segments.title: Magnetic tape to solid-state recorders
segments.summary: Early recorders used magnetic tape that overwrote itself about every thirty minutes. Solid-state memory replaced it, with greater capacity, durability, and recoverability. Recorders cost roughly ten to fifteen thousand dollars and are installed by manufacturers.

segments.title: What the recorders capture
segments.summary: Hundreds of sensors feed the Flight Data Acquisition Unit, which records up to around seven hundred parameters such as airspeed, altitude, cabin pressure, and switch positions. Cockpit microphones and in some newer planes video cameras capture the cockpit audio. Recorders are located at the tail because the rear is more likely to survive impact.

segments.title: Final words from cockpit recordings and FAA recording requirements
segments.summary: Hosts mention websites that collect last words from recordings and discuss how sensitive they are. They then cover FAA minimum parameter requirements, the cost dispute with the airline industry, and the stalled SAFE Act proposal for a second, rear-deployable recorder.

segments.title: Construction and layers of crash survivable memory unit
segments.summary: The memory unit has an aluminum housing around the memory modules, dry silica insulation for fire protection, and a stainless steel or titanium outer shell. The hosts describe its shape and the attached beacon handle.

segments.title: Crash survivability tests
segments.summary: The unit is tested by air-cannon impact into aluminum honeycomb, a spike drop from ten feet, a static crush of five thousand pounds per square inch, a fire test at about two thousand degrees Fahrenheit, deep-sea and saltwater immersion, and soaking in fluids like jet fuel.

segments.title: Finding, recovering, and analyzing black boxes
segments.summary: The underwater beacon activates on water contact and pings for about thirty days, detectable by sonar to around fourteen thousand feet. Air France Flight 447's recorders were found after two years in about twelve thousand feet of water. Recovered units are transported in seawater, data is downloaded or retrieved from memory modules, and investigators, manufacturers, and translators reconstruct the crash with simulations and wreckage reassembly.

segments.title: Black boxes in trains and cars
segments.summary: Recorders are used on trains and some car makers install them to track speed and driving for insurance. The hosts note controversy, including UK traffic tickets, and say the goal is learning from tragedy and preventing future accidents.

segments.title: Closing and sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts close the main content, mention the Cormack request, and sign off.
